body.title: River Silt and Sacred Straw: The Master Idol Artisans of Kumartuli
body.orientation: How generational potters along the Hooghly mold river clay and sacred earth into the divine icons of Durga Puja.

hero.alt: Artisan hands sculpting clay face of Goddess Durga in Kumartuli workshop

paragraphs.text: Kumartuli, located in North Kolkata along the Hooghly River, is a centuries-old artisanal enclave where hundreds of master potters sculpt thousands of clay idols annually for Durga Puja.
The sculpting process follows an ancient sequence: a bamboo and straw framework (Kathamo), coated in alluvial river silt (entel mati), and finished with smooth fine silt (bele mati).

sections.heading: Sacred soil and the Chakshu Daan ritual

paragraphs.text: Tradition requires incorporating a pinch of soil from the threshold of a courtesan's dwelling (punya mati), followed on Mahalaya by the solemn ritual of painting the goddess's eyes (Chakshu Daan).
Kumartuli embodies an ephemeral cycle of devotion: born from river silt, brought to life through community worship, and dissolved back into the river during immersion (Visarjan).

followUpQuestions: Why is immersion of clay idols into the Hooghly designed to be ecologically biodegradable?
How do women clay sculptors like China Pal challenge traditional patriarchal workshop boundaries?

claims.text: Kumartuli was founded along the riverfront by potters who migrated to supply clay vessels and idols to Kolkata.

evidence.excerpt: Kumartuli is a traditional potters' quarter in northern Kolkata known for sculpting clay idols for Durga Puja.

claims.text: Idols are sculpted around straw armatures using successive layers of Hooghly river clay.

evidence.excerpt: Artisans build the image around a bamboo frame using straw and clay gathered from the banks of the river Hooghly.

claims.text: The final ritual act of bestowing sight on the idol occurs on Mahalaya morning.

evidence.excerpt: The sacred act of painting the eyes of Goddess Durga, known as Chokhhu Daan, is traditionally performed on Mahalaya.

claims.text: The clay returns to the river upon immersion, completing an ecological and spiritual circle.

evidence.excerpt: The celebration concludes with the immersion of the clay idols into the river waters from which their clay was drawn.
